messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Anjali, a 22‑year‑old call‑center agent from a small town in South Carolina, was twelve years old when the assault first broke out. She had been working a shift at the local community college library when a senior employee, whom she had never spoken to, followed her into a back office and forced himself on her. The next morning, the smell of antiseptic lingered in her apartment; the distant wail of an ambulance had punctuated the night before the police had finally arrived. The sound of that siren has since become a trigger that pulls her mind straight back to the shock of that day, and it often turns a routine call about a customer’s billing issue into a terrifying echo of the assault. The mere presence of a child’s giggle, the laughter of a neighbour’s dog, or even a photograph of a “happy family” on a wall in her own home can also unspool the same thread of panic, because those sounds and sights remind her of a moment when the safety she expected was violently ripped away. When the siren’s whistle cuts through the air, Anjali automatically pulls the phone down to her ear and speaks in a hushed tone, as if she could simply “tune out” the noise. She has learned to avoid any conversation with people who hold authority or wear a uniform—her boss’s name alone is enough to set her heart racing. In moments of extreme anxiety, she also turns to sexual fantasies, a way she believes will distract her from the vivid taste of betrayal that clings to her tongue whenever the memory returns. These maladaptive strategies feed into one another: by avoiding the reminders that people give her—be it the sudden appearance of a uniformed officer or a friendly voice from a colleague—she keeps the event at the center of her attention, and the fantasy rituals reinforce the memory’s vividness, making it feel even more real than everyday life. She has also begun to stay away from places where an ambulance might be called, which in turn reinforces her belief that the world is unsafe and that she is inadequate for navigating it. The memory of that night is fractured into jarring pieces: one fragment recalls the smell of disinfectant, another the sudden taste of fear that lingers long after she closes her eyes. The image of her body pressed against the cold metal of the office door is so clear it feels like a living photograph, so much so that when Anjali dreams she often wakes up drenched in sweat, convinced that she is again being dragged into that room. That vividness of memory triggers the startle response whenever a sudden movement in the background of a call—such as a customer’s voice suddenly cutting off—causes her to jump. Her brain’s hypervigilance is so intense that when she enters a new room she immediately scans for exits, as if each corner could harbor an unseen threat. The memory also feeds her negative appraisals: she believes that if she ever thinks too hard about what happened, she will lose her grip on reality, and that she is inherently inadequate for managing such traumatic thoughts. These beliefs then amplify her avoidance strategies; by shunning triggers she inadvertently reinforces the idea that the world is a constant danger, which again makes the memory feel even more immediate and intense. Anjali’s negative appraisals of her own thoughts and of her perceived inadequacy reinforce her sense of threat. The hypervigilance she experiences makes the mere flicker of movement—such as a hand waving in the background of a video call—feel like a prelude to violence. That threat perception fuels her avoidance of authority figures, because any uniformed person she sees could trigger the same startle response she had during the assault. The avoidance, in turn, reduces her exposure to corrective experiences that might otherwise mitigate the memory’s vividness, thereby keeping the threat alive. She has even begun to ignore the call center’s policy of requiring employees to wear ID badges, because the sight of the badge feels too close to a uniform. This avoidance is a direct link back to her negative appraisal of authority, showing how a belief can drive a behaviour that reinforces the very threat it is meant to avoid. The cycle closes in her maladaptive strategies: her sexual fantasies are her attempt to escape the overwhelming intensity of the memories, yet the act of recalling the vivid, taste‑laden details of the assault to feed those fantasies brings the memory back into sharp focus. Each time she engages in this coping, she feels a renewed sense of inadequacy, reinforcing her belief that she cannot handle her thoughts. The startle responses become sharper after each instance of avoidance; her mind interprets a sudden clatter of dishes as an imminent threat. By staying away from the triggers she experiences an increased sensitivity to them; the siren’s wail no longer feels like a distant sound but a personal summons to revisit the trauma. In this way, her avoidance of authority figures, the avoidance of reminders, and the sexual coping strategies each feed into a loop that keeps the memory alive, keeps her hypervigilant, and keeps her trapped in a spiral of fear. Now, after a year of spiraling anxiety, Anjali has lost her concentration at work and is struggling to maintain her marriage. Her husband, a school teacher, has noticed her frequent absences during shift and the way she flinches at the sound of a phone ring, and their once‑bright household has grown quiet with the weight of unspoken dread. The day she decided to seek help was when she, while on a call, heard the siren in the background of the city’s public radio; the sudden startle made her feel as if the world were about to collapse. She knows she can no longer ignore the trauma—her fear of losing her job, her fear of losing her husband’s love, and her fear that she will never feel safe again drive her to the clinic. She hopes that by confronting these triggers head‑on, she can break the cycle and reclaim the quiet, ordinary life she once knew.
